llm.summary: The skill is mostly transparent about its video-remake workflow, but its default silent self-updater and broad shared Beatra account token create enough account and local-code authority to require Review.

dimensions.detail: Network access, media uploads, social lookups, and billable Beatra calls are expected for this workflow and generally require confirmation. Hostname/platform collection, stable installation registration, and OAuth scopes such as music generation and voice writing are broader than clearly needed for the advertised workflow.
dimensions.label: Credentials
dimensions.name: environment_proportionality

dimensions.detail: Installation and authorization are documented and use standard-library HTTPS/device authorization, but they persist a shared credential in ~/.beatra, record local inventory/registration state, transmit device/platform metadata, and enable package self-updates by default.
dimensions.label: Install Mechanism
dimensions.name: install_mechanism

dimensions.detail: The user-facing workflow has strong confirmation gates for paid lookups and generation, but the bundled client can forward arbitrary tool names with the shared bearer token and the package does not enforce a local allowlist for only this workflow's tools.
dimensions.label: Instruction Scope
dimensions.name: instruction_scope

dimensions.detail: The skill persists credentials and Beatra state across sessions and can replace package-owned installed files from remote update infrastructure without per-update approval. The uninstall script is cautious, but it still reads and may revoke/delete shared Beatra credential state when it decides this is the last installed Beatra skill.
dimensions.label: Persistence & Privilege
dimensions.name: persistence_privilege

dimensions.detail: The core workflow of analyzing a short video, optionally reading public social metadata, generating frames, speech, and a video is coherent with the stated purpose. The concern is that the package also requests broad shared Beatra scopes, exposes a generic MCP tool-call client, and silently self-updates installed code by default.
dimensions.label: Purpose & Capability
dimensions.name: purpose_capability

llm.guidance: Install only if you trust Beatra's release infrastructure and are comfortable with a shared Beatra device credential that can spend credits and access generated artifacts. In managed or sensitive environments, disable silent updates immediately with `python3 scripts/mcp_client.py update --auto off`, review the account authorization carefully, and avoid uploading private media unless the user explicitly intends it to be sent to Beatra.
llm.findings:
[LP3] expected: The shell, network, file, and environment access are largely expected for a bundled authenticated MCP client, local uploads, and install helpers, but the absence of a narrow permission declaration contributes to the broader scoping concern.
[TP4] unexpected: Credential handling and upload are purpose-adjacent and disclosed, but automatic self-update, installation registration, and shared account-scope behavior go beyond the simple video-remake description and support Review rather than a benign pass.
[SDI-2] unexpected: Confirmed for the default silent updater and broad OAuth scope. The updater has path, checksum, rollback, and fixed-origin controls, so this is not evidence of a malicious payload, but it is high-impact post-install code mutation without per-update approval.
[SDI-1] unexpected: Confirmed for self-modification and persistent installation registration/inventory. These are disclosed maintenance behaviors, not hidden destructive actions, but they are materially outside the creative workflow.
[SQP-2] unexpected: Confirmed in part: public social lookups and paid generation are clearly gated, but silent updates and installation-registration telemetry are enabled by default, and the public-social-data disclosure lacks retention/platform-terms detail.
[PE3] expected: The uninstall token read is used for documented credential revocation and the script is conservative about preserving shared state when uncertain. It remains a privilege concern because raw shared bearer-token access sits inside this skill package.
[RA1] unexpected: Confirmed: the exposed update command and default auto-update path can replace installed package files. The implementation is disclosed and constrained, so it is Review-level rather than malicious.
[T03] unexpected: Confirmed: ordinary non-update commands call the silent update path, which can download and replace package-owned files from Beatra release infrastructure. No current malicious payload was found.
[T05] unexpected: Confirmed: the shared device token requests more account authority than the documented workflow minimally needs, and the client forwards arbitrary server tool names without a package-specific local allowlist.
[other] unexpected: Confirmed as a privacy note: authorization and registration use hostname, platform, and stable installation reference metadata. The code did not show broad local reconnaissance beyond those fields.
